newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: UN chief calls on Zaire rebels to stop fighting.
newsitem.headline: UN chief calls on Zaire rebels to stop fighting.

text.p: U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan called on rebels in Zaire on Friday to stop fighting and start preparing for democracy.
At a news conference, Annan wondered whether Zaire's cancer-stricken leader Mobutu Sese Seko would step down, or be ready to continue talks for a transitional period without him.
"The scenario is very fluid and anything can happen," he said.

"We are also all aware that there is tremendous pressure on President Mobutu to step down. Would he step down and if so, when? If he doesn't step down, would he be prepared to continue the negotiations -- negotiations that would also lead to a transitional arrangements without him?"

The rebels, who control half the sprawling Central African nation including its economic heartland, have paused in their relentless advance and have given Mobutu until the weekend to signal that he is ready to quit.
Representatives of rebel leader Laurent Kabila and of Mobutu ended a first round of talks in South Africa last week with a statement recognising the need for talks on a peaceful solution and a truce.

South Africa's Deputy President Thabo Mbeki who hosted the talks told reporters in Washington on Thursday after meeting U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright that he hoped negotiations would resume early next week.
Mbeki said he expected the question of Mobutu's future to be on the agenda.
Annan urged the warring sides to get back to the negotiating table to agree to a full ceasefire and elections.
"I'd hope that when they come back together, they will be discussing transitional arrangements and eventually national elections for the selection of a leader of the country," Annan said.

"I cannot give you a timeframe. I think what's important is that we get all the interested to the table and discuss a cessation of hostilities, transitional arrangements and plan effectively for elections.
"I hope, and this is just a guess of mine, that in the next two to three months we should see some major development in the situation."
One by one, Western countries are ending their support for Mobutu, whom they once saw as the key to stability in Africa's third largest state.

The United States said this week it was time for him to go. France, the major European power in Africa, has dropped its belief that Mobutu could survive and called for an "orderly transition" of power. Belgium, the former colonial power, said Zaire was now in the hands of a military dictatorship.
